title: Identity and Access Management
summary: What identity and access management is, the problems it solves and the building blocks that make up an IAM platform like Fixiam.

children.text: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the set of processes and technology an organization uses to make sure the right people have the right access to the right resources, at the right time, and for the right reasons.
An IAM platform answers three questions for every request:
who is this?
what are they allowed to do?
and
should we let them do it right now?

cells: Verifies that a person is who they claim to be.
Decides what an authenticated person can access.
Creates, updates and removes access as people change.
Proves access is appropriate and reviewed.

children.text: Without a central IAM platform, every application keeps its own list of users and passwords. Access drifts as people change roles, former employees keep accounts, and nobody can say with confidence who can reach sensitive data.
Centralizing identity gives security teams one place to apply policy and gives employees one sign-in for everything they use.

terms.definition: The digital representation of a person, service or device, made up of a unique identifier and attributes.
Any entity that can be authenticated, such as a user, service account or device.
Giving each identity only the access it needs to do its job, and no more.

title: Authentication vs Authorization
summary: Authentication confirms who someone is. Authorization decides what they can do. Learn how the two differ and how Fixiam handles each.

children.text: People often use the words interchangeably, but they answer different questions and happen at different moments.

cells: What are you allowed to do?
Usually not, unless access is denied

children.text: Think of an office building. Showing your ID badge at reception is
authentication
: the guard confirms you are an employee. Whether your badge then opens the server room door is
authorization
: the building checks what your badge is allowed to open.

Fixiam authenticates people using the sign-in policy that applies to them, which may include a password, an authenticator or a biometric factor. Once a person is signed in, Fixiam authorizes access by checking which applications they are assigned to and which
roles
they hold inside each application.
A person can be fully authenticated and still be denied access to an application they are not assigned to. Fixiam logs both outcomes separately in the audit log.

terms.definition: Something a person presents to prove their identity, such as a password or a one-time code.
A named permission an application requests on behalf of a user, used in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

title: Roles and permissions
summary: How Fixiam uses roles to group permissions, both for administrators of Fixiam and for users inside connected applications.

children.text: A permission is a single action, such as
approve expense reports
. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as
Finance approver
. Assigning roles instead of individual permissions keeps access understandable as an organization grows.

sections.title: Two kinds of roles in Fixiam

children.text: Administrator roles
control what someone can do inside the Fixiam Admin Console, for example Super administrator, Help desk administrator or Read-only auditor.
Application roles
are passed to connected applications during sign-in so the application can decide what the user sees, for example Viewer, Editor or Owner.
Map application roles to Fixiam groups. When someone moves teams, their group membership changes and their application roles follow automatically.

terms.definition: Role-based access control. Access is granted through roles rather than directly to individuals.
Access every member of a group receives automatically, such as email for all employees.

title: Single Sign On
summary: Single Sign On (SSO) lets people sign in once with Fixiam and access all of their assigned applications without entering another password.

children.text: Single Sign On (SSO) is an authentication method that lets a person use one set of credentials to access many applications. Instead of each application checking a password it stores itself, the application trusts a central
identity provider
to confirm who the person is.
With Fixiam as your identity provider, employees sign in once in the morning and move between Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Slack and internal tools without being asked to sign in again.
Fewer passwords
People remember one strong password instead of reusing weak ones across dozens of tools.
Stronger security
MFA and sign-in policies are enforced in one place and apply to every connected application.
Faster offboarding
Suspending a user in Fixiam removes access to every SSO application at once.
Clear visibility
Every sign-in to every application is recorded in a single audit log.
SSO relies on a trust relationship between two parties that is set up once by an administrator:
The
identity provider (IdP)
authenticates the person. In this setup, that is Fixiam.
The
service provider (SP)
is the application the person wants to use.

The two exchange certificates or client secrets when you configure the integration. After that, every sign-in follows the same pattern: the application sends the person to Fixiam, Fixiam verifies them, and Fixiam sends back a signed message that the application can trust.

body.caption: Figure 1. A service provider initiated SSO flow. The application never sees the user's password.

children.text: The signed message is called an
assertion
in
SAML
and an
ID token
in
OpenID Connect
. Either way, the application checks the signature, reads who the user is, and starts a session.

sections.title: Where Fixiam fits into the flow

children.text: Fixiam is the identity provider in every SSO flow. It also connects to the systems your identities come from, so the person who signs in is always the current, correct version of that employee.

body.caption: Figure 2. Fixiam sits between where identities come from and the applications people use.

children.text: Because Fixiam is in the middle of every sign-in, it is also where you apply
multi factor authentication
adaptive policies
and device checks.
A sign-in can start in either place:
SP-initiated
: the person goes to the application first, as shown in Figure 1.
IdP-initiated
: the person starts in the Fixiam end user dashboard and selects an application tile.
Some applications only support one of these. The application page in the Fixiam catalog shows which ones are available.

terms.definition: The system that authenticates users and vouches for their identity. Fixiam is your IdP.
An application that relies on the identity provider to authenticate its users.
A signed SAML message from the IdP that states who the user is and what attributes they have.
The trust relationship between an IdP and an SP that makes SSO possible.
The period during which a user stays signed in without being asked for credentials again.

title: Multi Factor Authentication
summary: Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) asks people to prove their identity with more than one type of evidence, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

children.text: Multi Factor Authentication requires two or more independent pieces of evidence, called
factors
, before granting access. If one factor is compromised, for example a password in a phishing attack, the attacker still cannot sign in.
Factors are grouped by the kind of evidence they provide. A strong MFA policy combines factors from different groups.

cells: A secret only the user should know.
A device in the user’s possession.
Fixiam Verify push, TOTP code, security key
A physical characteristic of the user.

children.text: Two passwords are not multi factor. Both are something you know, so a single phishing page can capture both.
You decide when MFA is required through
authentication policies
. Common choices are:
Every sign-in to the Fixiam dashboard
Only when signing in from an unmanaged device or a new location
Every time someone opens a sensitive application, such as payroll
Policies that adjust based on context are described in
Adaptive authentication

Phishing-resistant factors such as security keys and biometrics give the strongest protection. TOTP codes are widely compatible and work offline. Most organizations enable two or three methods so people always have a fallback.
Start with Fixiam Verify push and TOTP for everyone, then require biometrics for administrators and privileged applications.

terms.definition: A category of evidence used to verify identity.
Time-based one-time password. A six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds.
The one-time process where a user registers an authenticator with Fixiam.
Asking for an additional factor in the middle of a session, before a sensitive action.

title: Adaptive authentication
summary: Adaptive authentication adjusts what Fixiam asks for at sign-in based on risk signals like device, location and behaviour.

children.text: Not every sign-in carries the same risk. An employee on a managed laptop in the office is lower risk than an unknown device in a new country. Adaptive authentication lets Fixiam reduce friction for low-risk sign-ins and add checks for high-risk ones.
Device
: is it enrolled and compliant with your device policy?
Network
: is the request from a trusted IP range?
Location
: is it a country the user normally signs in from?
Behaviour
: has this user failed sign-in several times recently?

cells: Allow with password or existing session
Require a phishing-resistant factor or deny

terms.definition: A piece of context about a sign-in that changes how risky it is likely to be.

title: SAML
summary: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML 2.0) is an XML-based standard that lets Fixiam securely tell an application who a user is.

children.text: SAML 2.0 is one of the two main standards used for
Single Sign On
. It has been widely adopted by enterprise applications for over a decade and is supported by most SaaS products.

sections.title: The key parts of a SAML integration

cells: A unique name for each party in the trust relationship.
Where Fixiam sends the assertion after sign-in.
Where the application sends users to sign in.
Lets the application verify the assertion was not tampered with.
The user identifier, usually the email address.

children.text: After Fixiam verifies a user, it sends a signed XML document to the application. This simplified example shows the parts an application reads.
Use whichever the application supports. If it supports both,
OpenID Connect
is usually simpler for modern web and mobile apps, while SAML is common for established enterprise software.

terms.definition: An XML file that contains an entity’s SAML settings, used to configure the other side quickly.
Assertion Consumer Service. The application endpoint that receives SAML assertions.

title: OpenID Connect
summary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on OAuth 2.0 that modern web and mobile applications use for Single Sign On.

children.text: OpenID Connect adds identity to OAuth 2.0. Where OAuth answers “can this app access this data?”, OIDC also answers “who is the user?” by returning a signed
ID token

cells: Proves who the user is. A signed JSON Web Token (JWT).
Lets the application call APIs on the user’s behalf.
Lets the application get new tokens without asking the user to sign in again.

children.text: Fixiam supports the authorization code flow with PKCE, which is the recommended flow for web, mobile and single page applications.

terms.definition: The public identifier Fixiam issues to an OIDC application.
The application URL that Fixiam returns the user to after sign-in.

title: SCIM
summary: System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) is a standard API for creating, updating and removing user accounts across systems.

children.text: SCIM defines a common REST API and JSON schema for user and group records. When two systems both speak SCIM, one can keep accounts in the other up to date automatically.
Inbound SCIM
: another system, such as an HR platform, pushes users into Fixiam.
Outbound SCIM
: Fixiam pushes users into a connected application, so accounts exist before the first sign-in.
SSO controls sign-in, but the account inside the application still needs to exist and be removed when someone leaves. SCIM closes that gap so
joiner, mover and leaver
events reach every application.

terms.definition: Creating an account in a target system.
Disabling or deleting an account when access is no longer needed.

title: Identity lifecycle management
summary: Identity lifecycle management keeps every account accurate from a person’s first day to their last, without manual tickets.

children.text: Every identity has a lifecycle. It is created when someone joins, changes as they move through the organization, and is removed when they leave. Lifecycle management automates each of these changes so access always matches a person’s current situation.
Automation starts with a trusted
identity source
, usually your HR system. When HR records a hire, transfer or termination, Fixiam receives the change and acts on it.

body.caption: Figure 2. Fixiam sits between where identities come from and the applications people use.

children.text: Account creation with the correct profile attributes
Group membership based on department, location and job title
Application assignment and provisioning through SCIM
Suspension and session revocation at termination
Automated deprovisioning is the most valuable part of lifecycle management. Former employees with active accounts are one of the most common audit findings.

terms.definition: Rules that decide which field in the source system fills which field in Fixiam.
A condition, such as department equals Finance, that adds users to a group automatically.

title: Joiner, Mover and Leaver
summary: Joiner, Mover and Leaver (JML) describes the three events in an employee’s lifecycle that should change their access.

children.text: JML is a simple model for thinking about access changes. Each event starts in your identity source and should end with the right access in every application.

body.caption: Figure 1. Each lifecycle event is triggered by a change in the identity source.

children.text: A joiner needs to be productive on day one. Fixiam creates the account from HR data before the start date, adds the person to groups based on their department, and sends an activation email on the morning they start.
Movers are the hardest event to get right manually. People collect access as they change roles, which leads to
privilege creep
. Fixiam recalculates group rules on every change so old access is removed as new access is granted.
When employment ends, every minute of remaining access is a risk. Fixiam suspends the account at the termination time in HR, revokes active sessions, and deprovisions SCIM-connected applications.
Schedule leaver processing for the end of the employee’s last working day, not the date HR enters the record, to avoid cutting off access early.

terms.definition: The gradual build-up of access a person no longer needs.

title: Identity sources
summary: An identity source is the system Fixiam treats as authoritative for who your people are, such as an HR platform or a directory.

children.text: Fixiam can hold users directly, but most organizations already manage people somewhere else. Connecting that system as an identity source means Fixiam stays in sync automatically.

cells: Organizations where HR is the first place a hire is recorded

children.text: You can connect several sources and decide which one wins for each attribute. A common pattern is HR for job details and Active Directory for usernames and groups.

terms.definition: The system whose data takes priority when two systems disagree.

title: Device management
summary: Fixiam Device Management enrolls company laptops and desktops, checks them against policy, and uses device trust in sign-in decisions.

children.text: Identity is only half of a trustworthy sign-in. The other half is the device. Device management lets you know which devices belong to your organization and whether they meet your security standards.
An administrator or user enrolls a device by installing the Fixiam Device Agent.
The agent reports device posture, such as disk encryption, OS version and screen lock.
Fixiam compares the posture with your
device policy
Sign-in policies can require a compliant device for sensitive applications.

cells: The agent is installed and reporting.
The device meets every rule in its policy.
At least one rule is failing. The user is told how to fix it.
The device has been removed from management.

terms.definition: The security state of a device at a point in time.
Using device posture as a signal in authentication decisions.

title: Access requests and approvals
summary: Access requests let people ask for the access they need, and route each request to the right approvers with a full audit trail.

children.text: Birthright access covers what everyone in a group needs. For everything else, people need a way to ask. Access requests replace emails and tickets with a consistent workflow that records who asked, who approved and why.
A user requests an application, role or group from the Fixiam dashboard.
Fixiam routes the request through the configured
approval levels
, such as manager then application owner.
When the final approver accepts, access is granted automatically, optionally for a limited time.
Requests can include an end date. Fixiam removes the access when the period ends, which is useful for contractors and project work.

terms.definition: One step in an approval chain. Each level can have one or more approvers.

title: Privileged Access Management
summary: Privileged Access Management (PAM) applies extra control to the small number of accounts that can change systems or reach sensitive data.

children.text: Privileged accounts can change configuration, read sensitive data or grant access to others. They are the most valuable target for attackers, so they deserve stronger controls than ordinary accounts.
Just-in-time access
: grant elevated access only when needed and remove it automatically.
Strong authentication
: require phishing-resistant factors for privileged roles.
Full audit
: record every privileged action for review.

terms.definition: Elevated access granted for a short, approved period.

title: Roll out SSO across your organization
summary: Move from separate application passwords to one Fixiam sign-in for every employee, from planning through to monitoring.
outcomes: Every priority application uses Fixiam for sign-in
Employees use one password and MFA everywhere
Sign-in activity is monitored in one place

children.text: List the applications your organization uses, who uses them and which SSO standard each one supports. Rank them by risk and number of users, and pick two or three for a pilot.
Start with an application that has many users and good SAML support, such as Microsoft 365 or Slack. An early win builds confidence.
SSO is only as good as the identities behind it. Connect the system that already knows who your employees are, so the right people exist in Fixiam before they sign in.
Add each pilot application from the Fixiam catalog. Catalog integrations come with recommended settings, which saves time and reduces mistakes.

stages.title: Configure SSO

children.text: Set up the trust between Fixiam and each application using SAML or OpenID Connect, whichever the application supports.

checklist: SSO configured for each pilot application

children.text: Assign the pilot group to each application. Use groups rather than individuals so access stays correct as people join and leave.

stages.title: Configure authentication requirements

children.text: Now that every sign-in goes through Fixiam, decide how strong it should be. Require MFA for the pilot group and consider stronger factors for sensitive applications.

checklist: MFA policy applied to pilot group

children.text: Test sign-in for each application from a private browser window, from both the Fixiam dashboard and the application’s own sign-in page. Test with a regular user, not only an administrator.
Keep a local administrator account in each application until testing is complete, so you can recover if SSO is misconfigured.

stages.title: Roll out to users

children.text: Expand assignments from the pilot group to wider groups in waves. Tell people what will change and when, and where to get help.

checklist: Direct sign-in disabled in each application

children.text: Watch sign-in success rates for each application in the first weeks. A spike in failures usually points to a mapping issue or users bypassing SSO.

title: Automate employee onboarding and offboarding
summary: Connect HR to Fixiam so joiners get access on day one and leavers lose it on their last day, without tickets.
audience: IT, HR operations and security teams
outcomes: New hires are created automatically from HR
Access follows people as they move

children.text: Agree with HR what each event means and when it should take effect.
Connect the HR system that records hires and terminations.
Decide which applications every employee, and every department, should get automatically.
Use SCIM so accounts in applications are created and removed with the identity.
Run a test termination and confirm the user is deactivated everywhere.
Turn on the source and review the first weeks of lifecycle events.

title: Strengthen authentication with MFA
summary: Introduce multi factor authentication for everyone, with phishing-resistant factors for the people and apps that need them most.
outcomes: Every user enrolled in at least one authenticator

children.text: Understand the difference between factors and which ones resist phishing.
Turn on at least two methods so users have a fallback.
Apply MFA to a pilot group with an enrollment grace period.
Expand the policy and track enrollment until everyone is covered.

title: Deploy Fixiam Device Management
summary: Enroll company devices, define compliance rules and require trusted devices for sensitive applications.

children.text: Learn how device posture becomes a sign-in signal.
Define what compliant means for each platform.
Enroll a pilot set of Windows and macOS devices, then the rest.
Find and fix non-compliant devices before enforcing.
Add a device requirement to sign-in policies for sensitive applications.

title: Connect your workforce identity source
summary: Bring your people into Fixiam from Active Directory, Google Workspace or HR, and keep them in sync.
outcomes: A single, accurate directory in Fixiam
Ongoing sync from the source of truth

children.text: Decide which system owns which attributes.
Connect a directory or HR system.
Run an import and check for duplicates.
Set a sync schedule and alerting.

title: Implement application access governance
summary: Give people a clear way to request access, route approvals, and prove access is appropriate.
outcomes: Consistent approvals with an audit trail

children.text: Understand birthright access, requests and approvals.
Agree approvers with application owners.
Add applications and roles to the access catalog.
Show approvers how to review requests.
Export access reports for compliance reviews.

title: Improved device management capabilities
summary: Device Management now supports macOS 15, bulk actions and a redesigned device detail page.

children.text: The device detail page now shows posture history for the last 30 days, the owner’s recent sign-ins and every policy rule with its current result. You can select several devices in
All devices
and retire them, change their owner or send a notification in one action.
The Fixiam Device Agent 4.2 adds support for macOS 15 and reduces battery usage on laptops by checking in less often when the device is idle.

title: Enhanced Google user import experience
summary: Google Workspace imports now show a preview with matched, new and skipped users before anything is created.

children.text: The import preview groups users into
New
Matched to existing
and
Skipped
, with the reason for every skip. You can filter by organizational unit or group before importing, and the import runs in the background so you can leave the page.

title: Active users no longer show an incorrect enrollment status
summary: Corrected an issue where active users could incorrectly display an enrollment status.

children.text: Some active users whose device had been retired showed
Enrollment pending
on their profile. The status is now calculated from active devices only. No action is needed.

title: Sessions are revoked when an authenticator is reset
summary: Resetting a user’s authenticators now also signs them out of every active session.

children.text: Previously, resetting authenticators only affected future sign-ins. Fixiam now revokes all sessions at the same time, so a lost or stolen device cannot keep using an existing session.

title: SeamlessHR connector
summary: Connect SeamlessHR as an identity source with built-in attribute mappings.

children.text: The new connector uses OAuth client credentials and supports joiner, mover and leaver processing out of the box. Custom fields can be mapped to any Fixiam attribute.

title: Faster portrait authentication
summary: Portrait verification now completes in under two seconds on most devices.

children.text: A new on-device liveness model reduces the time to verify and works better in low light.

title: SAML certificate rollover reminders
summary: Fixiam now emails application administrators 30, 14 and 3 days before a SAML signing certificate expires.

children.text: The application list also shows a warning badge on applications with a certificate expiring in the next 30 days.

title: Audit log filters keep their values after export
summary: Exporting from the audit log no longer clears your active filters.

children.text: Filters are now kept when you return from an export.

title: Multi-level approval chains
summary: Access requests can now pass through up to five approval levels, with escalation.

children.text: Each level can require one approver or all approvers, and can escalate to a fallback approver after a set number of days.

title: Clearer inbound SCIM errors
summary: SCIM responses now include a Fixiam error code and a link to troubleshooting.

children.text: Errors returned to SCIM clients include a
fixiamErrorCode
field that matches the troubleshooting section of the guide.

title: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 disabled
summary: All Fixiam endpoints now require TLS 1.2 or later.

children.text: Clients that only support older TLS versions can no longer connect. The Fixiam Agent and Device Agent have supported TLS 1.2 since 2023.

title: Breached password detection
summary: Password policies can now block passwords found in known breach datasets.

children.text: Turn on
Block breached passwords
in your password policy. Fixiam checks new passwords using a privacy-preserving lookup.

title: Application tiles load in the correct order
summary: Corrected an issue where custom tile order on the end user dashboard was sometimes ignored.

children.text: The dashboard now always respects the order a user sets.

title: Fingerprint authentication
summary: Users can now enroll a fingerprint as an authenticator on supported devices and scanners.

children.text: Fingerprint can be used as a second factor or, combined with a managed device, as a passwordless sign-in.

title: Application role priority
summary: When a user is in several groups, you can now choose which role wins.

children.text: Drag roles on the Roles tab to set priority.

title: SageHR connector
summary: Connect SageHR as an identity source.

children.text: Use an API key from SageHR to sync employees, teams and managers.

title: MFA required for all administrators
summary: Every administrator must now use MFA. Existing administrators were prompted to enroll.

children.text: The built-in Administrator policy cannot be disabled.

title: OpenID Connect applications
summary: Add custom OIDC applications with authorization code flow and PKCE.

children.text: OIDC applications support the openid, profile and email scopes, with custom claims.

title: CSV import handles accented names
summary: Names with accented characters now import correctly from UTF-8 CSV files.

children.text: Previously some characters were replaced with question marks.

title: Active Directory agent high availability
summary: Install more than one Fixiam Agent and Fixiam balances requests between them.

children.text: If an agent goes offline, delegated authentication continues through the remaining agents.

title: Fixiam Documentation launched
summary: A new home for Fixiam concepts, guides, journeys and release notes.

children.text: Documentation is now organized by what you are trying to do: learn, complete a task, or achieve a larger outcome.
